Renew our days as of old—<sup>22</sup>unless you have utterly rejected us, and you remain exceedingly angry with us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Look, and See Our Disgrace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last poem is a prayer from the whole community: Remember, O LORD, what has befallen us; look, and see our disgrace! (v. 1). They list what occupation has meant. Their inheritance belongs to foreigners (v. 2); they are orphans and widows (v. 3); they must buy their own water and firewood (v. 4) and are driven without rest (v. 5). They have begged bread from the great powers (v. 6), and they carry the consequences of their fathers' sins (v. 7). Slaves rule them (v. 8), getting bread risks their lives (v. 9), and famine burns their skin (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people may bring the concrete details of their distress to him and ask him to remember.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember, O LORD, what has befallen us; look, and see our disgrace! Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our homes to foreigners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember, O LORD, what has befallen us; look, and see our disgrace!

The first four poems each began with a cry — How — or with a single man's testimony. The last one begins with a prayer, and it is spoken by everyone. From the first verse to the last it is we, us, our. The whole community is on its knees.

Remember. When the Bible asks God to remember, it is not reminding him of something he has forgotten. It is asking him to act on what he knows. God remembered Noah, and the waters went down (Gen 8:1). God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant, and the exodus began (Exod 2:24).

A dying thief made the same prayer beside Jesus: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom (Luke 23:42). And he was heard that very day (Luke 23:43). There is no one too far gone to pray it.

Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our homes to foreigners.

The land had never been Israel's to sell. God said the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me (Lev 25:23). He had given it to them as an inheritance, family by family. Now it has been handed over to others, and the houses their grandparents built have other people living in them.

Christians are given a different inheritance, one that cannot be turned over to strangers: an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you (1 Pet 1:4). Houses can be lost. What God keeps for his people cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: We have become orphans, fatherless; our mothers are like widows. We must pay for the water we drink; the wood we get must be bought. Our pursuers are at our necks; we are weary; we are given no rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have become orphans, fatherless; our mothers are like widows.

Many of the men were dead or in exile, and the families left behind had no one to protect them. But it goes deeper than that. The people feel fatherless before God himself.

And yet God calls himself Father of the fatherless and protector of widows (Ps 68:5). Jesus, the night before he died, said to his friends, I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you (John 14:18). No one who belongs to Christ is ever truly an orphan.

We must pay for the water we drink; the wood we get must be bought.

Water from their own wells and wood from their own hills now had to be bought from the occupiers. It is a small detail, and it says everything about what it is to live under a conqueror.

Set it beside what God had given them at the beginning: cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant (Deut 6:11). They had received everything free and treated it as theirs by right. Now they paid for water. And set it beside what God offers still: Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price (Isa 55:1). Sin makes us pay for what grace gives away.

Our pursuers are at our necks; we are weary; we are given no rest.

The enemy is close behind, breathing down their necks. They are tired, and no one lets them stop. It is the curse Moses had described: among these nations you shall find no respite (Deut 28:65).

Weariness without rest is a picture of life under sin. And the one who can end it has said: Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: We have given the hand to Egypt, and to Assyria, to get bread enough. Our fathers sinned, and are no more; and we bear their iniquities. Slaves rule over us; there is none to deliver us from their hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have given the hand to Egypt, and to Assyria, to get bread enough.

To give the hand was to make a pact or to submit. For years Judah had turned to Egypt and Assyria for security, and Jeremiah had asked, what do you gain by going to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile? Or what do you gain by going to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates? (Jer 2:18). Now they hold out their hands to foreign powers simply to eat.

Every soul goes looking for bread somewhere. Only one place gives enough: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger (John 6:35).

Our fathers sinned, and are no more; and we bear their iniquities.

This line can sound like a complaint that the children are being punished for their parents. And it is true that sin's consequences pass down the generations. God himself said he visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children (Exod 34:7). The generation that caused the ruin was mostly dead, and their children were living in it.

But read on to verse 16: woe to us, for we have sinned! The people do not hide behind their fathers. They carry consequences they did not start, and they also confess sins they have committed themselves. Ezekiel had to correct the exiles who used the first truth to deny the second (Ezek 18:2-4).

Both halves are true for us too. We inherit damage from those who came before us, and we are responsible for our own sin. And the gospel answers both: of the Servant of the LORD it is said, he shall bear their iniquities (Isa 53:11). The iniquities we inherited and the iniquities we added, he carried.

Slaves rule over us; there is none to deliver us from their hand.

The people who once had their own king are now ordered about by servants of a foreign power — people of no standing, with authority over them. And there is none to deliver.

That is also the condition of every person under sin. Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin — and the slave cannot free himself. But the next words are the gospel: So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34, 36).

verseByVerse.quote: We get our bread at the peril of our lives, because of the sword in the wilderness. Our skin is hot as an oven with the burning heat of famine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We get our bread at the peril of our lives, because of the sword in the wilderness.

Going out to gather food meant risking raiders in the open country. Every meal cost a risk to someone's life.

Our skin is hot as an oven with the burning heat of famine.

Famine fever: bodies burning up from the inside. The poem does not let us forget that these are real people with real bodies.

Prayer like this is not unspiritual. God invites his people to tell him exactly what is wrong — the price of water, the danger of the fields, the fever in the body. Give us this day our daily bread (Matt 6:11) is a prayer Jesus taught. Nothing that concerns your life is too ordinary to bring to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer names the worst of it: women raped, princes hanged, elders shamed, young men and boys enslaved (vv. 11-13). The gate is empty, the music has stopped, and dancing has turned to mourning (vv. 14-15). Then the confession: The crown has fallen from our head; woe to us, for we have sinned! (v. 16). Their hearts are sick and their eyes dim, because Mount Zion is desolate and jackals prowl over it (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Behind every loss the people come back to the one cause they can confess: we have sinned.

verseByVerse.quote: Women are raped in Zion, young women in the towns of Judah. Princes are hung up by their hands; no respect is shown to the elders. Young men are compelled to grind at the mill, and boys stagger under loads of wood. The old men have left the city gate, the young men their music.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women are raped in Zion, young women in the towns of Judah.

The Bible names this. It does not soften it or look away, and neither should we. Rape was, and still is, a weapon of war.

That the verse stands in Scripture matters for every woman who has suffered this. God has seen it. He has written it into his own book as an outrage. It is not hidden from him and it is not unimportant to him. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit (Ps 34:18). And the church, which carries this book, must be a place where such suffering can be spoken of and is met with compassion, not silence.

Princes are hung up by their hands; no respect is shown to the elders.

The princes were hung up — executed or tortured, and put on display. The old men, whom the law commanded to be honoured — You shall stand up before the gray head and honor the face of an old man (Lev 19:32) — are treated with contempt.

The law said a hanged man is cursed by God (Deut 21:23). The princes of Judah were hung up as men under a curse. Paul quotes that law when he explains the cross: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13). The Prince of Peace was hung up too, so that the curse on his people could end.

Young men are compelled to grind at the mill, and boys stagger under loads of wood.

Grinding grain was the work of servants and prisoners. When the Philistines captured Samson, he ground at the mill in the prison (Judg 16:21). The strength of Judah's young men is being spent in slave labour, and even boys are loaded down like pack animals.

The old men have left the city gate, the young men their music.

The gate was where the elders sat to settle disputes and give counsel; now no one sits there. The young men used to play music; now there is none. Wisdom and joy have both gone out of the city. A community without the counsel of its old and the songs of its young is a community that has lost its life.

verseByVerse.quote: The joy of our hearts has ceased; our dancing has been turned to mourning. The crown has fallen from our head; woe to us, for we have sinned! For this our heart has become sick, for these things our eyes have grown dim, for Mount Zion which lies desolate; jackals prowl over it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The joy of our hearts has ceased; our dancing has been turned to mourning.

This is the exact reverse of the psalm: You have turned for me my mourning into dancing (Ps 30:11). Sin turned dancing into mourning. Only God can turn it back.

And he promised to. Through Jeremiah he had already said: Then shall the young women rejoice in the dance, and the young men and the old shall be merry. I will turn their mourning into joy (Jer 31:13). The very losses in these verses — young women, young men, the old, dancing, joy — are the ones God named in his promise.

The crown has fallen from our head; woe to us, for we have sinned!

The crown is their glory as a nation: the kingdom, the royal house, the honour of being God's people. It lies in the dust.

And here, at last, is the reason, spoken in the first person plural: woe to us, for we have sinned! After all the lament, all the detail, all the anguish, the prayer comes back to the heart of the matter. No blaming Babylon. No blaming the fathers. We have sinned.

That is where every road back to God begins. Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy (Prov 28:13). And the one who wore a crown of thorns gives his people a crown that cannot fall: Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life (Rev 2:10).

For this our heart has become sick, for these things our eyes have grown dim,

for Mount Zion which lies desolate; jackals prowl over it.

Of all the losses, this is the one that makes them heartsick: Mount Zion, the place where God chose to put his name, is desolate. Jeremiah had said God would make Jerusalem a heap of ruins, a lair of jackals (Jer 9:11). Now wild animals walk where the priests used to minister.

What they grieve most is not their comfort but the place of God's presence. That is a good test of any heart: what grieves you most? But there is comfort here too. The New Testament tells believers you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22). The Zion that jackals prowl was never the final one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–22 — But You, O LORD, Reign Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything on earth has fallen, but one throne has not: But you, O LORD, reign forever; your throne endures to all generations (v. 19). So the people dare to ask why God has forgotten them for so long (v. 20), and they pray: Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored! Renew our days as of old (v. 21) — unless you have utterly rejected us, and you remain exceedingly angry with us (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The book ends on a question only God can answer, and his answer is that he does not utterly reject his people.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, reign forever; your throne endures to all generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you, O LORD, reign forever; your throne endures to all generations.

But you. Everything in the first eighteen verses has fallen: the land, the homes, the fathers, the princes, the elders, the music, the crown, the temple mount. And here the prayer turns and looks up.

David's throne in Jerusalem is gone. The LORD's throne is not. But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever; you are remembered throughout all generations (Ps 102:12). The collapse of every earthly throne does not touch the throne of heaven.

That is the ground under everything else. If God still reigns, then what happened was not beyond his control, and what comes next is not beyond his power. When everything you built has come down, this is the sentence to hold on to.

And the New Testament shows whose throne it is. Of the Son he says, "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever" (Heb 1:8). At the end of the Bible, in the new Jerusalem, stands the throne of God and of the Lamb (Rev 22:3). The throne that endures to all generations belongs to the Lamb who was slain.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you forget us forever, why do you forsake us for so many days? Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored! Renew our days as of old— unless you have utterly rejected us, and you remain exceedingly angry with us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you forget us forever, why do you forsake us for so many days?

Because God reigns forever, the question becomes sharper, not softer: then why? If you are King, why have you left us so long? This is the language of the psalms: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? (Ps 13:1).

God had already answered this question through Isaiah. Zion said, "The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me." And God replied: Can a woman forget her nursing child...? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands (Isa 49:14-16).

And there was one who was truly forsaken. On the cross Jesus cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46). He was forsaken so that God could say to all who are in him: I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb 13:5).

Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored! Renew our days as of old—

Here is the real request, and look at its shape. Restore us to yourself — not first to the land, not first to prosperity, but to God. The deepest loss was never the city. It was God.

And that we may be restored. They know they cannot turn themselves around. If they are to come back, God must bring them back. It is Ephraim's prayer in Jeremiah: bring me back that I may be restored, for you are the LORD my God (Jer 31:18), and the psalm's: Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved! (Ps 80:3).

This is the heart of grace. Repentance is something we do, and it is also something God gives. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44). If you want to come back to God and find you cannot make your heart do it, pray this prayer. It is the prayer he answers.

Renew our days as of old. Not simply turn the clock back, but make new. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Cor 5:17).

unless you have utterly rejected us, and you remain exceedingly angry with us.

And so the book ends — not with an answer but with a fear. Unless. Unless it is too late. Unless you have finished with us.

It is a startling way to end a book of the Bible, and it is deliberate. Lamentations does not tie a bow on grief. It leaves the question hanging, because that is how grief really feels, and because the answer does not lie in the people's feelings. It lies in God.

And God had already answered. I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them (Lev 26:44). If the heavens above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth below can be explored, then I will cast off all the offspring of Israel (Jer 31:37). Paul asked the same question centuries later: has God rejected his people? By no means! (Rom 11:1).

The final answer is a person. Jesus said the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected (Mark 8:31). He was utterly rejected. He bore the exceeding anger of God. And because he did, he can make a promise that closes the question at the end of Lamentations for everyone who comes to him: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

5.title: Remember, O LORD
5.overview:
The last poem of Lamentations is a prayer from the whole community. It asks the LORD to remember and look at their disgrace, and it lists what their life has become: their inheritance given to foreigners, their families like orphans and widows, water and firewood that must be paid for, pursuers who give no rest. They have held out their hands to Egypt and Assyria for bread; they carry the consequences of their fathers' sins; servants rule them; food is gathered at the risk of their lives and famine burns their skin (vv. 1-10).

The prayer names the worst: women raped, princes hanged, elders dishonoured, young men and boys forced into slave labour. The gate is empty and the music has stopped; dancing has turned to mourning. The crown has fallen, and the people confess: woe to us, for we have sinned! Their hearts are sick because Mount Zion lies desolate and jackals prowl over it (vv. 11-18).

Then the prayer looks up. The LORD reigns forever, and his throne endures to all generations. So they ask why he has forgotten and forsaken them for so long, and they pray: Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored; renew our days as of old — unless you have utterly rejected us and remain exceedingly angry with us (vv. 19-22). The poem has twenty-two verses like the acrostics before it, but it does not follow the alphabet, and the book ends with its question still open.
5.theology:
To ask God to remember is to ask him to act on his covenant (v. 1; Gen 8:1; Exod 2:24; Luke 23:42). God's people may bring every concrete detail of their suffering to him (vv. 2-18).

Sin's consequences pass down the generations, yet each generation must confess its own sin; the Servant of the LORD bears both (vv. 7, 16; Exod 34:7; Ezek 18:2-4; Isa 53:11).

Scripture does not hide the violence done to the weak; God sees it and records it as an outrage (vv. 11-13; Ps 34:18).

When every earthly throne falls, the LORD's throne endures, and it is the throne of God and of the Lamb (v. 19; Ps 102:12; Heb 1:8; Rev 22:3).

Restoration is first restoration to God himself, and it is God's gift: he must turn his people if they are to be turned (v. 21; Jer 31:18; Ps 80:3; John 6:44).

God does not utterly reject his people (v. 22; Lev 26:44; Jer 31:37; Rom 11:1-2). Christ was rejected so that no one who comes to him will ever be cast out (Mark 8:31; John 6:37).
5.examples:
Paying for water from your own well.

Other families living in the houses your grandparents built.

Holding out your hand to a foreign power for a loaf.

An empty city gate and no music.

A crown in the dust, and the words: we have sinned.

Jackals walking where the priests once ministered.

But you, O LORD, reign forever.

A prayer to be turned by a people who cannot turn themselves.

A book that ends with unless — and a Saviour who answers it.
